import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 126

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/126](https://www.erdosproblems.com/126)
-/

open Filter

namespace Erdos126

def IsMaximalAddFactorsCard (f : ℕ → ℕ) : Prop := ∀ n,
    IsGreatest
      { m | ∀ (A : Finset ℕ), A.card = n →
        m ≤ (∏ ⟨a, b⟩ ∈ A.offDiag, (a + b)).primeFactors.card}
      (f n)

/--
Let $f(n)$ be maximal such that if $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ has $|A| = n$ then
$\prod_{a\neq b\in A}(a + b)$ has at least $f(n)$ distinct prime factors.
Is it true that $\frac{f(n)}{\log n} \to\infty$?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_126 : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ (f : ℕ → ℕ), IsMaximalAddFactorsCard f →
    Tendsto (fun n => f n / Real.log n) atTop atTop := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős and Turán proved [ErTu34] in their first joint paper that
$$
  \log n \ll f(n) \ll \frac{n}{\log n}
$$

[ErTu34] Erdős, Paul and Turan, Paul, _On a Problem in the Elementary Theory of Numbers_. Amer. Math. Monthly (1934), 608-611.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_126.variants.IsBigO
    (f : ℕ → ℕ)
    (hf : IsMaximalAddFactorsCard f) :
    ((fun (n : ℕ) => Real.log n) =O[atTop] fun (n : ℕ) => (f n : ℝ)) ∧
      (fun (n : ℕ) => (f n : ℝ)) =O[atTop] fun (n : ℕ) => n / Real.log n := by
  sorry

/--
Erdős says that $f(n) = o(\frac{n}{\log n})$ has never been proved.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_126.variants.isLittleO
    (f : ℕ → ℕ)
    (hf : IsMaximalAddFactorsCard f) :
    (fun (n : ℕ) => (f n : ℝ)) =o[atTop] (fun (n : ℕ) => n / Real.log n) := by
  sorry

end Erdos126

status_issues.source_status: The source now labels the problem PROVED (LEAN), solved affirmatively. It credits GPT-6 Astra with the stronger bound f(n) ≫ n^(1/2); Thomas Bloom posted the corresponding proof claim on 3 September 2026.
status_issues.evidence: https://www.erdosproblems.com/126 says “This has been solved in the affirmative and the proof verified in Lean” and records a last edit of 3 September 2026. https://www.erdosproblems.com/latex/126 explicitly states the stronger square-root lower bound. The linked exposition also concludes f(n)/log n → ∞.
status_issues.suggested_change: Change the category to research solved and replace answer(sorry) with answer(True). A formal_proof attribute can also be added after selecting the formalization linked by the source.

reformulations.difference: The source introduces one extremal function f; Lean universally quantifies over functions satisfying IsMaximalAddFactorsCard.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For each n, the attainable prime-factor counts form a nonempty subset of ℕ: Finset.range n provides an admissible set. Its minimum exists and is exactly the greatest universal lower bound in the definition. These minima give a unique qualifying function. The scratch file proves existence and uniqueness, equivalence with attained minima, and the generic equivalence (∀ f, IsMaximalAddFactorsCard f → P f) ↔ P extremal. Thus the universal quantification is neither weaker nor vacuous.

reformulations.difference: The 1934 paper works with positive integers, whereas Finset ℕ also permits zero.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Let f₀ and f₊ be the minima for nonnegative and positive integers respectively. Then f₀(n) ≤ f₊(n) ≤ f₀(n+1): positive sets are admissible nonnegative sets, and any (n+1)-element nonnegative set contains n positive elements whose sum-product prime support is a subset of the original support. The scratch file proves this sandwich. Since log(n+1)/log n → 1 and ((n+1)/log(n+1))/(n/log n) → 1, both Big-O bounds are equivalent under the two conventions. The same comparison preserves the main limit and the little-o variant. The full asymptotic equivalences were not mechanized.

review.notes: All four declarations were checked. /workspace/review/scratch.lean compiles without errors or warnings. In addition to the equivalence checks, it proves that every off-diagonal sum-product is nonzero, so Nat.primeFactors' zero default is unreachable; verifies f(0)=f(1)=f(2)=0 under the nonnegative convention; and checks eventual logarithm positivity and the little-o/ratio-limit equivalence. Division elaborates over ℝ, and the exceptional logarithm values at 0 and 1 do not affect atTop statements. Ordered pairs do not change distinct prime support. The new lower bound does not settle the little-o upper-bound variant, which the source still leaves unresolved.
